events.summary: Solid first cut with high confidence across most fields. Native status, range, bloom season, size, wildlife value, and butterfly nectar records are all well-sourced from FNPS, Florida Wildflower Foundation, Fairchild, and UF/IFAS Charlotte County. The gall-midge ecology is confirmed by peer-reviewed literature. Edibility is based on a single ethnobotanical source (Cornucopia II via Eat the Weeds / Austin's Florida Ethnobotany); toxicity is Green by omission from all poison-control databases searched.

events.feedback: What a perfect selection for the park! Planting Sea Ox-eye Daisy along the ponds at Palma Sola Botanical Park is an absolute masterstroke for a few key reasons, and this card tells that story beautifully.🌟 Why This Plant is a Perfect Fit for PSBPThe Immediate Hyper-Local Connection: The profile smartly points out that Palma Sola Bay is literally right outside the gates. Telling visitors that the exact same native species they see in the park is currently stabilizing the shoreline of the bay creates a brilliant "aha!" moment.Built for the Environment: Thriving in sand, muck, brackish water, and coastal flooding means this selection will easily handle the punishing, salty conditions along the pond edges where ordinary landscaping turns yellow and dies.The Butterfly & Bee Benefit: While it doesn't serve as a larval host, blooming much of the year means it provides a reliable, steady nectar buffet for the park's coastal pollinators.🛠️ Final Sanity Check & Edits for the DirectorThe text is
events.summary: The edibility flag is corrected from Red to Yellow — the leaves are documented as edible but bitterly impractical, so Red (unsafe/toxic) was a false alarm and Green (safe food) would be misleading. Quick Hits bullet 3 is tightened to eliminate the near-verbatim overlap with the first More Information paragraph on water-storing leaves, while keeping the specific, visitor-facing salt-shedding detail.

events.feedback: Please add to the quick hits that this is one of the many pond plants the park volunteers with the help of Bright Futures high school students are planting across the whole park to shore up the banks of the ponds which have eroded over time. The park is actively working two grants from Tampa Bay and Sarasota Bay Estuary Programs, for which they are very grateful
events.summary: A single quick hit was added to reflect the park's active pond-bank restoration effort, crediting Bright Futures high school student volunteers and the two estuary program grants. All other fields are unchanged.
